title: Footprints without Feet
status: DRAFT — for review by an English teacher before any question is approved
source: Written against NCERT Class X English supplementary reader ‘Footprints without Feet’ (jefp1, reprint 2026-27), read from the chapter PDFs, to the CBSE English Language and Literature (184) question paper design for 2025-26. The board paper sets no extract from this book; the extracts here are practice. Extracts are quoted from the book and checked word for word by scripts/check-english-questions.mjs.

questions.stem: Mrs Pumphrey calls Tricki's recovery 'a triumph of surgery'. Why is this phrase ironic?

options.text: The operation was a failure and Tricki had to be treated again.
No operation was done; Tricki recovered through a strict diet, exercise and the company of other dogs.
Mr Herriot had operated on the wrong dog.
Tricki recovered before he ever reached the surgery.

questions.explanation: The narrator says Tricki 'had no medicinal treatment of any kind'. He was given no food for two days and then ran about with the dogs. The 'surgery' was only the vet's premises, so calling it a triumph of surgery is the opposite of what happened.

questions.stem: Mrs Pumphrey thought Tricki was 'suffering from malnutrition' and gave him malt, cod-liver oil and Horlicks. What does this reveal about her?

options.text: She had carefully followed the vet's advice.
She wanted to save money on his regular meals.
She knew he was overfed but did not care.
Her love was blind: she misread overeating as weakness and made the problem worse.

questions.explanation: Tricki was 'hugely fat, like a bloated sausage', yet she believed he needed 'little extras between meals to build him up'. She also admits she could not keep him off sweet things: 'I can't bear to refuse him.' Her indulgence caused the illness.

questions.stem: When the eggs, wine and brandy arrive, 'the real possibilities of the situation began to dawn on the household.' What does this suggest about the narrator's tone?

options.text: It is gently humorous: the vet and his partners enjoy the gifts meant for Tricki.
It is angry, because Mrs Pumphrey is wasting good food.
It is worried, because Tricki may be harmed by the wine.
It is sad, because the household misses Tricki's mistress.

questions.explanation: The narrator describes 'two eggs each for breakfast', lunch as 'a ceremonial occasion' with wine, and brandy 'reverently drunk' — 'days of deep content'. The gifts meant 'to enrich Tricki's blood' are enjoyed by the humans, and the tone is light and amused.

questions.stem: Mrs Pumphrey 'set off, head down, along the road, as if determined to put the new regime into practice immediately.' In this sentence, 'regime' means

options.text: a new set of rules for her household staff
a government that controls a country
a prescribed course of diet and exercise
a medicine the vet had given her

questions.explanation: The vet has just told her to 'cut his food right down and give him more exercise' and keep him 'on a very strict diet'. The glossary gives 'regime' as a 'prescribed course of exercise and diet'.

questions.stem: When Tricki goes home, the narrator helps bring out 'the beds, toys, cushions, coats and bowls, none of which had been used.' What does this detail most suggest?

options.text: The narrator had forgotten to unpack Tricki's belongings.
The other dogs would not let Tricki use his things.
Tricki had been too ill to play with his toys.
Tricki did not need any of his luxuries; the simple life of an ordinary dog cured him.

questions.explanation: Tricki spent the fortnight running with the gang, 'fighting like a tiger for his share at mealtimes and hunting rats'. The unused luxuries show that the pampering was never what he needed.

questions.extract: Mrs Pumphrey hastened to explain, "He was so listless, Mr Herriot. He seemed to have no energy. I thought he must be suffering from malnutrition, so I have been giving him some little extras between meals to build him up, some malt and cod-liver oil and a bowl of Horlicks at night to make him sleep -- nothing much really."

parts.prompt: The word 'listless', as used in the extract, means

options.text: restless and noisy
hungry all the time
lacking energy and enthusiasm
unable to sleep

parts.answer: (c) lacking energy and enthusiasm — she explains it herself: 'He seemed to have no energy.'

parts.prompt: What did Mrs Pumphrey wrongly believe was the cause of Tricki's condition?
parts.answer: Malnutrition — she thought he was not getting enough nourishment.

parts.prompt: The words 'nothing much really' at the end of her explanation show that Mrs Pumphrey

options.text: does not see that the extras are part of the problem
has stopped feeding Tricki altogether
is lying about how little she feeds him
wants the vet to prescribe more food

parts.answer: (a) — she treats malt, cod-liver oil and Horlicks between meals as trifles, not seeing that overfeeding is what is making Tricki ill.

parts.prompt: Why did the narrator feel that Tricki needed to be taken away from Mrs Pumphrey? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: Mrs Pumphrey could not refuse Tricki food — she gave him sweets and extras and 'had to relent' on the diet. Tricki's 'only fault was greed', so the vet saw that the only way to save him was to get him out of the house. (1 mark: her indulgence; 1 mark: the need to remove him to cure him.)

questions.extract: The word 'convalescing' seemed to do something to Mrs Pumphrey. She started to bring round fresh eggs, two dozen at a time, to build up Tricki's strength. For a happy period my partners and I had two eggs each for breakfast, but when the bottles of wine began to arrive, the real possibilities of the situation began to dawn on the household.

parts.prompt: 'Convalescing' means

options.text: getting worse
being operated on
refusing food
recovering from an illness

parts.answer: (d) recovering from an illness.

parts.prompt: Why did Mrs Pumphrey send fresh eggs to the surgery?
parts.answer: To build up Tricki's strength.

parts.prompt: Who actually ate the eggs Mrs Pumphrey sent?

options.text: Tricki and the other dogs
The narrator and his partners
Mrs Pumphrey's own staff
Tristan alone

parts.answer: (b) — 'my partners and I had two eggs each for breakfast'.

parts.prompt: What were 'the real possibilities of the situation' that dawned on the household? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: The household realised that while Tricki stayed, Mrs Pumphrey would keep sending luxuries meant for him — eggs, wine to 'enrich Tricki's blood', later brandy — which they themselves could enjoy. (1 mark: the gifts would keep coming; 1 mark: the vets, not Tricki, would enjoy them.)

questions.extract:
The entire staff was roused and maids rushed in and out bringing his day bed, his night bed, favourite cushions, toys and rubber rings, breakfast bowl, lunch bowl, supper bowl. Realising that my car would never hold all the stuff, I started to drive away. As I moved off, Mrs Pumphrey, with a despairing cry, threw an armful of the little coats through the window. I looked in the mirror before I turned the corner of the drive; everybody was in tears.
Out on the road, I glanced down at the pathetic little animal gasping on the seat by my side. I patted the head and Tricki made a brave effort to wag his tail. "Poor old lad," I said. "You haven't a kick in you but I think I know a cure for you."

parts.prompt: The long list of things the maids bring — 'his day bed, his night bed ... breakfast bowl, lunch bowl, supper bowl' — mainly shows

options.text: how carefully the household prepared Tricki for hospital
how absurdly Tricki had been pampered
that the vet had asked for all these things
that Tricki needed special equipment because he was ill

parts.answer: (b) — a small dog with three bowls, two beds and a heap of toys is a comic picture of excessive indulgence; the narrator simply drives off because his car 'would never hold all the stuff'.

parts.prompt: What did Mrs Pumphrey throw through the car window as the narrator drove away?
parts.answer: An armful of Tricki's little coats.

parts.prompt: The narrator's words, 'You haven't a kick in you but I think I know a cure for you', show that he

options.text: feels sorry for Tricki and is confident he understands what is wrong
believes Tricki is too weak to survive
is planning a difficult operation
is angry with Tricki for his greed

parts.answer: (a) — 'Poor old lad' and the pat on the head show sympathy, and 'I think I know a cure' shows he already has a plan.

parts.prompt: What does the scene of Tricki's departure tell us about Mrs Pumphrey's household? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: The whole household revolves around the dog: 'the entire staff was roused' and maids rushed about with his belongings. Mrs Pumphrey's despairing cry and 'everybody was in tears' show an exaggerated, emotional attachment, as if Tricki were leaving for ever. (1 mark: staff and belongings fussing over the dog; 1 mark: the exaggerated grief.)

questions.stem: How did Tricki recover at the surgery without any medicine? Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: For two days he was given no food but plenty of water.
He was kept with the other dogs and began to show interest in his surroundings.
He had to compete with the dogs at mealtimes and ran about with them all day, joining their scrimmages.
In two weeks he became 'a lithe, hard-muscled animal'.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: The fasting and the exercise and company of the other dogs, linked to his recovery. Any two or three value points, correctly linked.

rubric.descriptor: Clear, connected sentences in about 40–50 words, with accurate grammar and spelling.

questions.stem: Mr Herriot is both tactful and full of common sense. Support this with evidence from the story. Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: Common sense: he saw that Tricki's 'only fault was greed' and cured him with diet and exercise, not medicine.
He took a firm line and removed Tricki from the house, since that was 'the only way to save him'.
Tact: he dodged Mrs Pumphrey's questions about cushions and coats, telling her only that Tricki was 'convalescing rapidly'.
He did not tell her that her own indulgence was the cause, and let her believe in 'a triumph of surgery'.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: One piece of evidence for common sense and one for tact (1 mark each).

questions.stem: Describe the scene when Mrs Pumphrey came to collect Tricki. What does it show? Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: She arrived in a huge car — 'about thirty feet of gleaming black metal' — with a chauffeur, trembling and anxious.
Tricki leapt from the narrator's arms into her lap and licked her face, barking.
The beds, toys, cushions, coats and bowls were returned, none of them used.
In tears, she thanked him for 'a triumph of surgery' — showing her deep love, and that she never understood the real cure.

rubric.descriptor: Details of the reunion and what it shows about Mrs Pumphrey or Tricki.

rubric.label: Expression

questions.stem: Do you think Tricki was happy to go home? Give reasons from the story. Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: Yes: when he saw his mistress he 'took off from my arms in a tremendous leap' into her lap, licking her face.
He clearly loved Mrs Pumphrey.
But at the surgery 'he had never had such a time in his life', running and hunting rats with the gang.
A balanced answer may note that his old pampered life could make him ill again.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: A clear view supported by at least two details from the story.

valuePoints: Tricki had become 'hugely fat, like a bloated sausage with a leg at each corner'.
His eyes were bloodshot and rheumy, and his tongue lolled from his jaws.
Mrs Pumphrey had given him extras between meals and could not refuse him cream cakes and chocolates.
He had had little exercise: there had been no ring-throwing since Hodgkin, the gardener, was down with lumbago.

valuePoints: Mrs Pumphrey sent fresh eggs, bottles of wine and brandy to build up Tricki's strength.
The narrator and his partners enjoyed them: 'days of deep content' with eggs, midday wine and brandy by the fire.
But he knew Mrs Pumphrey was suffering without her dog.
Tricki had recovered, so he felt compelled to phone her and send him home.

questions.stem: Mrs Pumphrey loved Tricki, yet her love made him ill. Some parents, too, give children whatever they ask for. Write an article for your school magazine, in about 100–120 words, titled 'When Love Says Yes Too Often'. Draw on the story, and suggest how caring for someone can include saying no.
valuePoints: Article format: title, and an opening that sets out the idea.
Mrs Pumphrey's indulgence — sweets, extras between meals, no exercise — and its result: Tricki fell seriously ill.
The cure came from firmness: a strict diet, exercise and the company of other dogs.
Overindulgence of children (junk food, gadgets, no limits) can harm health and habits.
A reasoned conclusion that real care sometimes means setting limits.

questions.stem: Tricki needed no medicine: running, playing and competing with other dogs made him 'a lithe, hard-muscled animal' in two weeks. Many students today spend long hours sitting with screens and snacks. Write a speech, in about 100–120 words, to be delivered in your morning assembly on the topic 'Play Is the Best Medicine'. Use Tricki's recovery as an example, and suggest practical ways in which students can build activity into their day.

Tricki's illness came from overeating and no exercise; he recovered without medicine through activity and company.
A comparison with students' habits: long screen time, junk food, little outdoor play.
Practical suggestions: a daily game or walk, taking the stairs, breaks from screens, playing with friends.
A conclusion that small, regular changes in habit protect health.

questions.stem: The narrator says 'it's difficult to rob a careless man'. Why does he find robbing Anil difficult?

options.text: Anil kept his money locked away safely.
Anil was strong enough to catch him.
Anil trusted him completely, and a trusting man may not even notice the loss, which takes the pleasure out of it.
Anil had very little money worth stealing.

questions.explanation: Anil 'was the most trusting person I had ever met. And that is why it was so difficult to rob him.' A careless man 'doesn't even notice he's been robbed and that takes all the pleasure out of the work.'

questions.stem: At the end, 'the smile came by itself, without any effort.' What does this change in Hari Singh's smile suggest?

options.text: His smile was now genuine, not a trick to win someone's confidence.
He was relieved that Anil had not discovered the theft.
He was planning to steal from Anil again.
He was pleased to be paid more than before.

questions.explanation: Earlier he used 'my most appealing smile' deliberately to manipulate Anil. At the end Anil 'knew' but forgave silently, and the smile came 'without any effort' — a sign of real gratitude and change.

questions.stem: How did Hari Singh realise that Anil knew about the theft?

options.text: Anil counted the money in front of him.
Anil told him he had seen him leave at night.
The police came to the room in the morning.
The fifty-rupee note Anil gave him was still wet from the night's rain.

questions.explanation: The notes had got damp in the rain while Hari Singh sat in the bazaar. When he took the note from Anil, 'it was still wet from the night's rain' — so Anil must have found the returned money. 'He knew.'

questions.stem: Hari Singh says, 'I took a new name every month. That kept me ahead of the police and my former employers.' What does this reveal about him?

options.text: He had probably cheated or robbed earlier employers and was used to escaping the consequences.
He was ashamed of his real name and wanted a better one.
He changed jobs often because employers did not pay him.
The police were searching for him because of one crime he regretted.

questions.explanation: He needed to stay 'ahead of' both the police and his 'former employers', which suggests a habit of stealing from those he worked for. He calls himself 'an experienced and fairly successful hand' at thieving.

questions.stem: At the station, Hari Singh says, 'I hesitated -- for some reason I can't explain -- and I lost the chance to get away.' Which is the most reasonable interpretation of this hesitation?

options.text: He was afraid of being caught without a ticket.
He was too tired from running to jump aboard.
His feelings for Anil and what he stood to lose were already pulling him back, though he did not yet understand it.
He had decided to take a later train to Lucknow.

questions.explanation: He 'had never bought a ticket in my life', so fear of the ticket office is unlikely. Soon afterwards he thinks of Anil's sadness at 'the loss of trust' and of the sentences he would no longer learn, which suggests his hesitation came from something he could not yet name.

questions.extract: Anil was asleep. A beam of moonlight stepped over the balcony and fell on the bed. I sat up on the floor, considering the situation. If I took the money, I could catch the 10.30 Express to Lucknow. Slipping out of the blanket, I crept up to the bed. Anil was sleeping peacefully. His face was clear and unlined; even I had more marks on my face, though mine were mostly scars.

parts.prompt: The word 'unlined', as used in the extract, suggests that Anil

options.text: was very old
showed no sign of worry or anxiety
was badly injured
had not shaved

parts.answer: (b) showed no sign of worry or anxiety.

parts.prompt: Where did the narrator plan to go with the stolen money?
parts.answer: To Lucknow, by the 10.30 Express.

parts.prompt: The contrast between Anil's 'clear' face and the narrator's scars suggests that

options.text: Anil was younger than the narrator
the narrator had been in a wrestling match
Anil had never had to work
the narrator, though younger, had led a harder, rougher life

parts.answer: (d) — the fifteen-year-old thief bears scars, while the trusting Anil, about 25, sleeps peacefully without a care.

parts.prompt: Why did the narrator decide it was time to steal the money? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: He had not done 'real work' for a month and felt out of practice. He also told himself that Anil would only waste the money on his friends, and did not even pay him. (1 mark: out of practice; 1 mark: his excuses about Anil.)

questions.extract: In my short career as a thief, I had made a study of men's faces when they had lost their goods. The greedy man showed fear; the rich man showed anger; the poor man showed acceptance. But I knew that Anil's face, when he discovered the theft, would show only a touch of sadness. Not for the loss of money, but for the loss of trust.

parts.prompt: According to the narrator, how did a poor man react to being robbed?

options.text: With fear
With anger
With acceptance
With sadness

parts.answer: (c) — 'the poor man showed acceptance'.

parts.prompt: What, according to the narrator, would Anil be sad about?
parts.answer: The loss of trust, not the loss of money.

parts.prompt: The phrase 'I had made a study of men's faces' shows that the narrator was

options.text: an observant judge of people
a student of painting
afraid of being recognised
careless about his work

parts.answer: (a) an observant judge of people — he had watched closely how different people react to loss.

parts.prompt: How does this understanding of Anil help explain why the narrator later returned the money? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: He knew Anil valued trust more than money, so the theft would hurt Anil as a betrayal. Along with his wish to learn to read and write, this made him go back and put the notes under the mattress. (1 mark: Anil values trust; 1 mark: link to returning the money.)

questions.extract: I hurried back to the room feeling very nervous, for it is much easier to steal something than to return it undetected. I opened the door quietly, then stood in the doorway, in clouded moonlight. Anil was still asleep. I crept to the head of the bed, and my hand came up with the notes. I felt his breath on my hand. I remained still for a minute. Then my hand found the edge of the mattress, and slipped under it with the notes.

parts.prompt: The word 'undetected', as used in the extract, means

options.text: unharmed
unwillingly
unpunished by the police
without being noticed

parts.answer: (d) without being noticed — he wants to put the money back without Anil waking and finding out.

parts.prompt: Where did the narrator put the notes back?
parts.answer: Under the edge of Anil's mattress, where Anil had kept them.

parts.prompt: 'I felt his breath on my hand. I remained still for a minute.' These lines create a feeling of

options.text: tension, as he fears Anil may wake
calm, as the task is almost over
anger at Anil for sleeping so lightly
pride in his skill as a thief

parts.answer: (a) — his hand is so close that he feels Anil's breath, and he freezes, which builds suspense.

parts.prompt: Why does the narrator find it harder to return the money than to steal it? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: Stealing was his familiar skill, done 'without a sound'. Returning it is new to him: he is 'very nervous' because being caught now would cost him Anil's trust and the chance to learn — things he has begun to value. (1 mark: stealing was practised and easy; 1 mark: returning risks losing what he now cares about. Accept other well-reasoned answers.)

questions.stem: Why did Hari Singh return the money to Anil? Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: He realised he could no longer learn to write whole sentences if he ran away.
'Whole sentences… could one day bring me more than a few hundred rupees'; he wanted to be 'a clever and respected man'.
Stealing was simple, but 'just as simple to be caught'.
He knew Anil would feel the loss of trust, and he had nowhere else to go.

rubric.descriptor: The wish for education and respect as the main reason, with at least one further reason from the story.

He worried about his next cheque but went out to celebrate as soon as it arrived.
He was 'the most trusting person' the narrator had met: he gave him a key and did not mind his small profit on the shopping.

questions.stem: 'Trust can change a person more than punishment can.' Write a speech, in about 100–120 words, to be delivered in your school assembly on this topic. Use 'The Thief's Story' as your example, and say what young people can learn about trusting others and being trustworthy.
valuePoints: Speech format: greeting, topic introduced, closing thanks.
Anil trusted Hari Singh with a key and his money, taught him and did not report him.
That trust, and the hope of education, made the thief return the money and change.
Punishment might have hardened him; trust gave him a reason to be better.
What students can learn: to give others a fair chance, and to value the trust placed in them.

questions.stem: At Drury Lane, Griffin 'callously attacked the shopkeeper from behind' and robbed him. What does the word 'callously' reveal about Griffin?

options.text: He was too frightened to face the shopkeeper.
He was clumsy because of the cold.
He cared nothing for the harm he did to others.
He regretted hurting a man who had helped him.

questions.explanation: 'Callously' means without pity or concern. Griffin attacks an innocent shopkeeper simply to escape unseen, and then robs him of all his money — he puts his own needs above anyone else's safety.

questions.stem: Why did Mr and Mrs Hall decide to look into the scientist's room early that morning?

options.text: His door, usually shut and locked, was wide open, and the chance seemed too good to miss.
They heard him shouting for help.
The constable had asked them to search it.
He had asked Mrs Hall to change the bedclothes.

questions.explanation: The text says the door was 'wide open. Usually it was shut and locked, and he was furious if anyone entered his room. The opportunity seemed too good to be missed.' Curiosity about their secretive guest drew them in.

questions.stem: Why did the villagers suspect the strange scientist of the burglary at the clergyman's home?

options.text: Someone had seen him near the clergyman's study.
The clergyman recognised his bandages.
He had threatened the clergyman the day before.
He suddenly had ready cash soon after admitting he had no money.

questions.explanation: 'Suspicion grew even stronger when he suddenly produced some ready cash, though he had admitted not long before that he had no money.' Nobody had seen the thief, so the sudden money was the clue.

questions.stem: At Iping, 'a stranger of such uncommon appearance set all tongues wagging.' This means that the stranger

options.text: made the villagers gossip about him
frightened the villagers into silence
talked a great deal to everyone at the inn
was laughed at openly by the villagers

questions.explanation: 'Set tongues wagging' is an idiom for causing people to talk and gossip. A stranger arriving in winter was unusual, and his bandages and dark glasses made him even more a subject of talk.

questions.stem: When his stolen money ran out, Griffin 'pretended, however, that he was expecting a cheque to arrive at any moment.' What does this show?

options.text: He was a successful scientist who was paid by cheque.
He was embarrassed and planned to leave the inn at once.
He was ready to deceive Mrs Hall to keep his rooms without paying.
He trusted Mrs Hall enough to tell her the truth about his money.

questions.explanation: The word 'pretended' shows the cheque was a lie. Griffin had been living on stolen money, and now deceives the woman who had excused his 'strange habits and irritable temper'.

questions.extract:
Griffin, the scientist, had carried out experiment after experiment to prove that the human body could become invisible. Finally he swallowed certain rare drugs and his body became as transparent as a sheet of glass -- though it also remained as solid as glass.
Brilliant scientist though he was, Griffin was rather a lawless person. His landlord disliked him and tried to eject him. In revenge Griffin set fire to the house. To get away without being seen he had to remove his clothes. Thus it was that he became a homeless wanderer, without clothes, without money, and quite invisible -- until he happened to step in some mud, and left footprints as he walked!

parts.prompt: Griffin's body became invisible because he

options.text: wore a special sheet of glass
swallowed certain rare drugs
set fire to his landlord's house
removed all his clothes

parts.answer: (b) — 'he swallowed certain rare drugs and his body became as transparent as a sheet of glass'.

parts.prompt: Which word in the extract means 'to force someone to leave a place'?

parts.prompt: Griffin had to remove his clothes because

options.text: they had caught fire
they were muddy
he wanted to test his invisibility
he had to get away without being seen

parts.answer: (d) — 'To get away without being seen he had to remove his clothes.'

parts.prompt: Which action in the extract best shows that Griffin was 'rather a lawless person'? Explain in 30–40 words.

questions.extract:
All of a sudden Mrs Hall heard a sniff close to her ear. A moment later the hat on the bedpost leapt up and dashed itself into her face. Then the bedroom chair became alive. Springing into the air it charged straight at her, legs foremost. As she and her husband turned away in terror, the extraordinary chair pushed them both out of the room and then appeared to slam and lock the door after them.
Mrs Hall almost fell down the stairs in hysterics. She was convinced that the room was haunted by spirits, and that the stranger had somehow caused these to enter into her furniture.

parts.prompt: The 'sniff close to her ear' was most probably made by

options.text: the invisible Griffin standing in the room
a spirit haunting the furniture
Mr Hall, who had a cold
the clergyman hiding behind the door

parts.answer: (a) — Griffin, invisible without his clothes and bandages, was in the room; it was he who threw the hat and moved the chair.

parts.prompt: What did Mrs Hall believe had happened to her furniture?
parts.answer: That the room was haunted by spirits which the stranger had somehow caused to enter her furniture.

parts.prompt: The word 'hysterics', as used in the extract, means

options.text: loud laughter at a joke
a state of deep sleep
a fit of uncontrollable fear and excitement
a sudden fall caused by illness

parts.answer: (c) a fit of uncontrollable fear and excitement.

parts.prompt: Why did the events in the room seem supernatural to Mr and Mrs Hall, though they had a simple explanation? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: The room looked empty and his clothes and bandages lay about, so they could not see anyone. The hat and chair seemed to move by themselves, but it was the invisible Griffin throwing them. (1 mark: why it seemed supernatural; 1 mark: the real explanation.)

questions.extract: Mr Jaffers, the constable, now arrived, and was quite surprised to find that he had to arrest a man without a head. But Jaffers was not easily prevented from doing his duty. If a magistrate's warrant ordered a person's arrest, then that person had to be arrested, with or without his head. There followed a remarkable scene as the policeman tried to get hold of a man who was becoming more and more invisible as he threw off one garment after another.

options.text: angry
humorous
sorrowful
fearful

parts.prompt: Why was it hard for Jaffers to get hold of the man?

parts.prompt: 'Jaffers was not easily prevented from doing his duty' shows that the constable was

confused and helpless
careless about the law
determined and dutiful

parts.prompt: What does this scene show about the way Griffin used his invisibility? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: Griffin used invisibility to resist a lawful arrest. Throwing off his clothes to vanish made the constable helpless, showing that he placed himself above the law. (1 mark: used it to escape arrest; 1 mark: shows his lawless attitude.)

questions.stem: In the seventh grade Ebright entered a county science fair and won nothing. What did the loss teach him?

options.text: That science fairs favoured older students
That the winners had tried to do real experiments, not simply make a neat display
That he should give up studying insects
That frog tissues were a better subject than butterflies

questions.explanation: His entry was slides of frog tissues. 'He realised the winners had tried to do real experiments, not simply make a neat display', and he resolved: 'for the next year's fair I would have to do a real experiment.'

questions.stem: Ebright worked in summer 'at the entomology laboratory of the Walter Reed Army Institute of Research'. Why was an entomology laboratory a fitting place for him?

options.text: It studied the chemistry of rocks and fossils.
It trained army officers in debating.
Entomology is the study of insects, and his research was on monarch butterflies.
It was the laboratory where the Proceedings were printed.

questions.explanation: The glossary defines entomology as 'the study of insects'. Ebright's research on the gold spots of the monarch pupa was insect research, so the laboratory suited his work.

questions.stem: Mr Weiherer said Richard 'was competitive, but not in a bad sense'. What did he mean?

options.text: Richard wanted to do the best job he could, not win merely for a prize.
Richard never entered competitions he might lose.
Richard helped his rivals so that they would win.
Richard competed only in debating, never in science.

questions.explanation: Mr Weiherer explained: 'Richard wasn't interested in winning for winning's sake or winning to get a prize. Rather, he was winning because he wanted to do the best job he could.'

questions.stem: The writer says that having their work published in the journal as college students was 'like making the big leagues at the age of fifteen and hitting a home run your first time at bat'. What does this comparison convey?

options.text: That Ebright was a better baseball player than a scientist
That the achievement came very young and at the very first attempt, which is extremely rare
That the journal published the paper only because Ebright was well known in sports
That Ebright had worked on the paper since he was fifteen

questions.explanation: It was 'the first time this important scientific journal had ever published the work of college students'. The footnote explains the comparison: getting a paper published so young is like 'scoring a home run while batting for the first time' — a rare success, early and at the first try.

questions.stem: Of his eighth grade project on the disease that kills monarch caterpillars, Ebright said, 'I didn't get any real results. But I went ahead and showed that I had tried the experiment. This time I won.' What does this suggest about what the fair valued?

options.text: Only projects that proved their theory could win a prize.
A neat display mattered more than the experiment behind it.
Winning depended mainly on help from a well-known scientist.
A genuine attempt at a real experiment counted, even without a conclusive result.

questions.explanation: The year before, his display of frog-tissue slides won nothing because 'the winners had tried to do real experiments, not simply make a neat display'. In the eighth grade he got no real results but 'showed that I had tried the experiment' and won — so the honest attempt at a real experiment is what counted.

questions.extract:
From the first he had a driving curiosity along with a bright mind. He also had a mother who encouraged his interest in learning. She took him on trips, bought him telescopes, microscopes, cameras, mounting materials, and other equipment and helped him in many other ways.
"I was his only companion until he started school," his mother said. "After that I would bring home friends for him. But at night we just did things together. Richie was my whole life after his father died when Richie was in third grade."
She and her son spent almost every evening at the dining room table. "If he didn't have things to do, I found work for him -- not physical work, but learning things," his mother said. "He liked it. He wanted to learn."

parts.prompt: The phrase 'a driving curiosity' suggests that Ebright's curiosity was

options.text: occasional and easily lost
limited to cars and machines
strong enough to push him constantly to learn more
forced on him by his mother

parts.answer: (c) — 'driving' means a powerful force that keeps pushing him forward.

parts.prompt: Name any two things Ebright's mother bought him to encourage his interest in learning.
parts.answer: Any two of: telescopes, microscopes, cameras, mounting materials (and other equipment).

parts.prompt: The work his mother found for him in the evenings was

options.text: learning things
household chores
physical exercise
tagging butterflies for money

parts.answer: (a) — 'not physical work, but learning things'.

parts.prompt: Why was Ebright's mother such an important influence in his life? Answer in 30–40 words.

questions.extract:
"Richard was competitive," Mr Weiherer continued, "but not in a bad sense." He explained, "Richard wasn't interested in winning for winning's sake or winning to get a prize. Rather, he was winning because he wanted to do the best job he could. For the right reasons, he wants to be the best."
And that is one of the ingredients in the making of a scientist. Start with a first-rate mind, add curiosity, and mix in the will to win for the right reasons. Ebright has these qualities. From the time the book, The Travels of Monarch X, opened the world of science to him, Richard Ebright has never lost his scientific curiosity.

questions.extract:
The next year his science fair project was testing the theory that viceroy butterflies copy monarchs. The theory was that viceroys look like monarchs because monarchs don't taste good to birds. Viceroys, on the other hand, do taste good to birds. So the more they look like monarchs, the less likely they are to become a bird's dinner.
Ebright's project was to see whether, in fact, birds would eat monarchs. He found that a starling would not eat ordinary bird food. It would eat all the monarchs it could get. (Ebright said later research by other people showed that viceroys probably do copy the monarch.) This project was placed first in the zoology division and third overall in the county science fair.

parts.prompt: According to the theory Ebright tested, viceroys look like monarchs because

options.text: both butterflies migrate to Central America
monarchs do not taste good to birds
birds cannot see the colours of butterflies
viceroys taste worse than monarchs

parts.answer: (b) — 'viceroys look like monarchs because monarchs don't taste good to birds'.

parts.prompt: Which bird did Ebright find would eat all the monarchs it could get?
parts.answer: A starling.

parts.prompt: The sentence in brackets tells the reader that

no one else ever studied viceroys and monarchs
Ebright gave up the study of butterflies after this project
later research by other people showed that viceroys probably do copy the monarch

parts.answer: (d) — '(Ebright said later research by other people showed that viceroys probably do copy the monarch.)'

parts.prompt: Why might the starling's behaviour have been an unexpected finding for the theory being tested? Answer in 30–40 words.

Yet the starling refused ordinary bird food and ate all the monarchs it could get, which does not fit that idea. (1 mark: what the theory assumed; 1 mark: how the starling's behaviour went against it. Accept a well-argued alternative.)

questions.stem: At the end of 'The Necklace', Mme Forestier says, 'Mine were false. They were not worth over five hundred francs!' What makes this ending ironic?

options.text: Matilda had never really lost the necklace at the ball.
The Loisels spent ten years of hardship paying for a necklace that was almost worthless.
Mme Forestier had known all along that the necklace had been replaced.
Loisel had secretly bought a false necklace to save money.

questions.explanation: The Loisels paid thirty-six thousand francs for a replacement and 'it has taken us ten years to pay for it'. Only at the end do they learn the original 'was not worth over five hundred francs' — their sacrifice was for nothing, the opposite of what they believed.

questions.stem: When her husband brings home the invitation to the Minister's party, Matilda throws it 'spitefully upon the table'. What does this reaction reveal about her?

options.text: She is dissatisfied because she feels she has nothing fit to wear among rich people.
She dislikes the Minister and does not want to meet him.
She is too shy to go to any party at all.
She is angry that her husband has come home late.

questions.explanation: She at once asks, 'What do you suppose I have to wear to such a thing as that?' and weeps because she has 'no dress'. Her reaction comes from her discontent with her modest means, not from anything about the party itself.

questions.stem: When Matilda asks for four hundred francs for a dress, Loisel 'turned a little pale' but said, 'Very well. I will give you four hundred francs.' What does this show about him?

options.text: He suspected that she would waste the money.
He was angry and gave the money only to end the quarrel.
He hoped she would change her mind and stay at home.
He was willing to give up his own wish for her happiness.

questions.explanation: He turned pale because 'he had saved just this sum to buy a gun' to join hunting parties the next summer. Giving the money anyway shows a loving, self-sacrificing husband.

questions.stem: After a week of searching for the necklace, the writer says, 'And Loisel, older by five years, declared, "We must replace this jewel."' What does 'older by five years' suggest?

options.text: Loisel's birthday had fallen during that week.
Loisel was five years older than his wife.
The strain and worry of that week had aged him visibly.
Loisel had lied about his age to the lenders.

questions.explanation: Only a week has passed. The phrase is not literal: the fruitless search — the police, the cab offices, the advertisement — and the loss of all hope had worn him down so much that he seemed five years older.

questions.stem: When Mme Loisel returned the jewels, Mme Forestier said to her 'in a frigid tone, "You should have returned them to me sooner, for I might have needed them."' The word 'frigid' here means

options.text: cold and unfriendly
loud and angry
shaky and frightened
warm and grateful

questions.explanation: 'Frigid' literally means very cold. Used of a tone, it means cold and unfriendly — Mme Forestier is displeased that the necklace has been kept so long.

questions.extract:
She suffered incessantly, feeling herself born for all delicacies and luxuries. She suffered from the poverty of her apartment, the shabby walls and the worn chairs. All these things tortured and angered her.
When she seated herself for dinner opposite her husband who uncovered the tureen with a delighted air, saying, "Oh! the good potpie! I know nothing better than that...," she would think of elegant dinners, of shining silver; she thought of the exquisite food served in marvellous dishes. She had neither frocks nor jewels, nothing. And she loved only those things.

parts.prompt: The word 'incessantly', as used in the extract, means

silently
continuously
deliberately

both husband and wife dislike the food they can afford
the husband is greedy and the wife is generous
Matilda has cooked an elegant dinner for her husband

parts.answer: (a) — he is delighted with a potpie, while she thinks of 'elegant dinners' and 'shining silver'.

parts.prompt: How did Matilda's belief that she was 'born for all delicacies and luxuries' affect her life? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: It made her permanently unhappy. The shabby walls and worn chairs 'tortured and angered her', she dreamt of luxuries she could not have, and she could not enjoy the simple life and loving husband she had. (1 mark: her constant unhappiness; 1 mark: an example from the extract.)

questions.extract:
Mme Loisel now knew the horrible life of necessity. She did her part, however, completely, heroically. It was necessary to pay this frightful debt. She would pay it. They sent away the maid, they changed their lodgings; they rented some rooms in an attic.
She learned the odious work of a kitchen. She washed the dishes. She washed the soiled linen, their clothes and dishcloths, which she hung on the line to dry; she took down the refuse to the street each morning and brought up the water, stopping at each landing to catch her breath.

parts.prompt: The word 'odious' is closest in meaning to

options.text: simple
unfamiliar
well-paid
hateful

parts.answer: (d) hateful — very unpleasant.

parts.prompt: What steps did the Loisels take to cut down their expenses?
parts.answer: They sent away the maid, changed their lodgings and rented some rooms in an attic.

parts.prompt: 'She did her part, however, completely, heroically.' This line presents Matilda as

options.text: careless and still dreaming of luxury
determined to meet her responsibility for the debt
bitter and blaming her husband for the loss
waiting for Mme Forestier to forgive the debt

parts.answer: (b) — 'It was necessary to pay this frightful debt. She would pay it.'

parts.prompt: How is the life described in the extract different from the life Matilda had dreamt of? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: She had dreamt of elegant dinners, frocks and jewels. Now she lives in an attic, washes dishes and linen, carries refuse and water, and is breathless on the stairs — a life of hard labour and poverty. (1 mark: her dream; 1 mark: her new life.)

questions.extract:
The day of the ball arrived. Mme Loisel was a great success. She was the prettiest of all -- elegant, gracious, smiling and full of joy. All the men noticed her, asked her name, and wanted to be presented.
She danced with enthusiasm, intoxicated with pleasure, thinking of nothing but all this admiration, this victory so complete and sweet to her heart.
She went home towards four o'clock in the morning. Her husband had been half asleep in one of the little salons since midnight, with three other gentlemen whose wives were enjoying themselves very much.

parts.prompt: The phrase 'intoxicated with pleasure', as used in the extract, means

options.text: tired out by dancing
ill after the party food
anxious about the necklace
carried away by delight

parts.prompt: Where was Matilda's husband while she danced, and since when?

parts.prompt: 'This victory so complete and sweet to her heart' refers to

the admiration she won from everyone at the ball
her husband's promotion at the office
getting the dress for four hundred francs

parts.prompt: How does the evening described here differ for Matilda and her husband, and what does the difference suggest? Answer in 30–40 words.

questions.stem: 'The teacher's voice was so soft and soothing! In all her life she had never been called like that.' Why did this moment matter so much to Bholi?

options.text: The teacher had promised to find her a good husband.
She was glad to be allowed to go home early.
It was the first time anyone had spoken to her with gentleness and respect.
She recognised the teacher as someone from her own family.

questions.explanation: At home Bholi was neglected and called a fool, and other children mimicked her stammer. The text says 'It touched her heart' — the teacher's kindness was new to her, and it gave her the courage to try to speak.

questions.stem: Bholi's mother says, 'Send Bholi to school. As it is, there is little chance of her getting married... Let the teachers at school worry about her.' What does this show about how her family saw Bholi?

options.text: They believed school would help her find a rich husband.
They saw her as a burden with little future worth planning for.
They thought she was the cleverest of their daughters.
They wanted her to become a teacher one day.

questions.explanation: Her mother had just asked, 'If girls go to school, who will marry them?' She sends Bholi only because she thinks Bholi's chances of marriage are already poor, so the teachers can 'worry about her'. It shows neglect, not hope for her.

questions.stem: Throughout the story she is called Bholi, 'the simpleton', but near the end the writer says, 'And Sulekha said in a voice that was calm and steady'. Why is her real name used at this point?

options.text: She is no longer the simpleton; she has become a confident, sensible young woman.
Her father has changed her name after the wedding was cancelled.
The guests at the wedding did not know her pet name.
The teacher has asked everyone to call her by her school name.

questions.explanation: 'Bholi' meant 'the simpleton'. By now she speaks 'without even the slightest stammer', rejects a greedy bridegroom and calmly plans to care for her parents and teach. Using 'Sulekha' marks this change.

questions.stem: When her father said he would take her to school, Bholi 'remembered how a few days ago their old cow, Lakshmi, had been turned out of the house and sold', and shouted in terror. Why did this memory frighten her?

options.text: She was afraid her father would punish her for losing the cow.
She feared that she too was being sent away from home for good.
She had been told that the school was built where the cow was sold.
She wanted to go and look for Lakshmi instead.

questions.explanation: Bholi 'did not know what a school was like'. Having just seen Lakshmi turned out and sold, she feared she too was being taken away and got rid of — which also hints at how little she felt wanted at home.

questions.stem: At the end, in the teacher's eyes 'was the light of a deep satisfaction that an artist feels when contemplating the completion of her masterpiece'. What is the 'masterpiece'?

options.text: The grand wedding that she had helped to arrange
The picture book she gave Bholi on the first day
The primary school that had become a high school
Bholi herself — a frightened, stammering child grown into a confident young woman

questions.explanation: The teacher had encouraged Bholi from her first day, promising that 'people will listen to you with respect'. Seeing Bholi speak clearly, refuse Bishamber and plan to teach, she feels like an artist who has finished her finest work — the change in Bholi is her masterpiece.

questions.extract: "Bholi." The teacher's voice was so soft and soothing! In all her life she had never been called like that. It touched her heart. "Get up," said the teacher. It was not a command, but just a friendly suggestion. Bholi got up. "Now tell me your name." Sweat broke out over her whole body. Would her stammering tongue again disgrace her? For the sake of this kind woman, however, she decided to make an effort. She had such a soothing voice; she would not laugh at her.

parts.prompt: 'It was not a command, but just a friendly suggestion.' The teacher's manner is in sharp contrast to that of

options.text: the Tehsildar, who opened the school
her sister Champa, who gave her a dress
the headmistress, who refused to admit her
her father, who had shouted at her and called her a fool

parts.answer: (d) — that morning Ramlal had shouted, 'What's the matter with you, you fool?'

parts.prompt: Why did sweat break out over Bholi's body when she was asked her name?
parts.answer: She was afraid her stammering tongue would disgrace her again and the girls would laugh at her.

parts.prompt: What made Bholi decide to 'make an effort' to speak?

options.text: She wanted to impress the other girls in the class.
She was afraid she would be punished.
She trusted that this kind woman would not laugh at her.
Her father had ordered her to answer the teacher.

parts.answer: (c) — 'For the sake of this kind woman... she would not laugh at her.'

parts.prompt: How does this moment mark the beginning of a change in Bholi? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: For the first time someone treats her gently, and that trust makes her try to speak despite her fear. With the teacher's encouragement she manages to say her name, and a new confidence and hope begin. (1 mark: the teacher's kindness winning her trust; 1 mark: the first step towards confidence.)

questions.extract:
Once again the veil was slipped back from the bride's face, but this time her eyes were not downcast. She was looking up, looking straight at her prospective husband, and in her eyes there was neither anger nor hate, only cold contempt.
Bishamber raised the garland to place it round the bride's neck; but before he could do so, Bholi's hand struck out like a streak of lightning and the garland was flung into the fire. She got up and threw away the veil.

parts.prompt: The word 'downcast', as used in the extract, means

options.text: full of tears
looking downwards
tightly closed
shining with joy

parts.answer: (b) looking downwards.

parts.prompt: Name the figure of speech in 'Bholi's hand struck out like a streak of lightning'.
parts.answer: Simile — her movement is compared to a streak of lightning, showing how swift and sudden it was.

parts.prompt: Bholi felt 'cold contempt' for Bishamber because he

options.text: had demanded five thousand rupees after seeing her pock-marks
was old and walked with a limp
came from another village
had arrived with a noisy brass band

parts.answer: (a) — he humiliated her father for money; Bholi calls him 'a mean, greedy and contemptible coward'. She had been willing to marry 'this lame old man', so (b) is not the reason.

parts.prompt: What change in Bholi is shown by 'this time her eyes were not downcast'? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: Earlier she kept her face lowered and accepted what was decided for her. Now she looks straight at Bishamber — she has found the confidence and self-respect to judge him and to refuse the marriage. (1 mark: the earlier submissiveness; 1 mark: her new confidence and self-respect.)

questions.extract:
Bholi did not know what exactly a school was like and what happened there, but she was glad to find so many girls almost of her own age present there. She hoped that one of these girls might become her friend.
The lady teacher who was in the class was saying something to the girls but Bholi could understand nothing. She looked at the pictures on the wall. The colours fascinated her -- the horse was brown just like the horse on which the Tehsildar had come to visit their village; the goat was black like the goat of their neighbour; the parrot was green like the parrots she had seen in the mango orchard; and the cow was just like their Lakshmi.

parts.prompt: Bholi's hope that 'one of these girls might become her friend' suggests that

options.text: she had many friends in the village already
she wanted someone to help her with lessons
she longed for the companionship she had not had
she wished to leave the school quickly

parts.answer: (c) — other children had made fun of her, and she talked very little; she longed for a friend.

parts.prompt: What did the brown horse in the picture remind Bholi of?
parts.answer: The horse on which the Tehsildar had come to visit their village.

parts.prompt: The word 'fascinated', as used in the extract, means

options.text: frightened
confused
bored
held her attention with delight

parts.prompt: What does Bholi's response to the pictures suggest about her, even though she was called 'the simpleton'? Answer in 30–40 words.

questions.stem: 'The Book That Saved the Earth' is a satire. What is the chief target of its humour?

options.text: The poor design of Martian spaceships
The Earthlings' habit of eating sandwiches
Historians who exaggerate the past
A vain leader who believes he is never wrong and misreads what he does not understand

questions.explanation: Think-Tank calls himself 'most powerful and intelligent creature in the whole universe', makes everyone chant that he 'is never wrong', and then mistakes books for sandwiches and nursery rhymes for military threats. The play mocks such arrogance.

questions.stem: On hearing 'The cow jumped over the moon', Think-Tank fears 'an interplanetary attack of millions of cows'. What is his basic mistake?

options.text: He does not believe that cows exist on Earth.
He thinks the rhyme is about Mars.
He takes a nonsense rhyme for children literally.
He confuses the moon with the sun.

questions.explanation: 'Hey diddle diddle' is a nursery rhyme meant for fun — even Oop laughs at 'The dish ran away with the spoon'. Think-Tank reads it as fact and concludes Earthlings have taught 'their domesticated animals musical culture and space techniques'.

questions.stem: How does Noodle manage to correct Think-Tank's mistakes without offending him?

options.text: He contradicts him openly in front of the space crew.
He offers his correction humbly, as a small bit of data, and lets Think-Tank take the credit.
He sends secret messages to the invasion fleet.
He waits until Think-Tank has left before speaking.

questions.explanation: Noodle says 'an insignificant bit of data floated into my mind' and 'a cloudy piece of information is twirling around in my head'. Think-Tank then adopts the idea as his own: 'Naturally. That was my next point.'

questions.stem: When Oop laughs at 'Mistress Mary, quite contrary', Think-Tank snaps, 'Stop! This is no time for levity.' What does 'levity' mean here?

options.text: Lack of seriousness
Lack of intelligence
Floating in the air
Disobeying an order

questions.explanation: The glossary gives 'levity' as 'tendency to treat serious matters without respect; lack of seriousness'. Think-Tank believes the rhyme is a grave discovery, so he objects to Oop laughing at it.

questions.stem: The Historian ends by saying there is 'still one book that the Martians can never bring themselves to read' — Mother Goose. Why is this a humorous ending?

options.text: Mother Goose is too difficult for Martians to read.
The Martians have no copy of it in their library.
Noodle, the new ruler, has banned it throughout Mars.
A children's book of rhymes is the one book the Martians still cannot face.

questions.explanation: The Martians learned to read and have a model library in Marsopolis, yet the one book they avoid is a 'dusty old book of nursery rhymes'. The humour lies in the gap between how harmless the book is and the lasting fear it caused.

questions.extract:
NOODLE: Sir, sir. Great and Mighty Think-Tank. I beg your pardon, but an insignificant bit of data floated into my mind about those sandwiches.
THINK-TANK: It can't be worth much, but go ahead. Give us your trifling bit of data.
NOODLE: Well, sir, I have seen surveyor films of those sandwiches. I noticed that the Earthlings did not eat them. They used them as some sort of communication device.
THINK-TANK: (haughtily) Naturally. That was my next point. These are actually communication sandwiches. Think-Tank is never wrong. Who is never wrong?

parts.prompt: The word 'trifling', as used by Think-Tank, means

options.text: unimportant
confusing
secret
surprising

parts.answer: (a) unimportant.

parts.prompt: What had Noodle noticed in the surveyor films?
parts.answer: That the Earthlings did not eat the 'sandwiches' (books) but used them as some sort of communication device.

parts.prompt: 'Naturally. That was my next point.' This reply shows that Think-Tank

options.text: is grateful to Noodle for his help
has studied Earth carefully
is only joking with Noodle
cannot admit a mistake and takes credit for Noodle's idea

parts.answer: (d) — he had just ordered Oop to eat a book, yet claims the correction as his own.

parts.prompt: Think-Tank first dismisses Noodle's data and then adopts it. What does this reveal about the two characters? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: Think-Tank is arrogant and vain: he calls Noodle's data 'trifling' and insists he is 'never wrong'. Noodle is humble and tactful, and more observant than his master, correcting him without hurting his pride. (1 mark: Think-Tank; 1 mark: Noodle.)

questions.extract: THINK-TANK: (screaming and holding his head) It's me! It's my Great and Mighty Balloon Brain. The Earthlings have seen me, and they're after me. "Had a great fall!" -- That means they plan to capture Mars Central Control and me! It's an invasion of Mars! Noodle, prepare a space capsule for me. I must escape without delay. Space people, you must leave Earth at once, but be sure to remove all traces of your visit. The Earthlings must not know that I know.

parts.prompt: Think-Tank believes the picture of Humpty Dumpty is of him because

options.text: the rhyme mentions Mars by name
Noodle tells him that it is his portrait
Humpty Dumpty, like him, has a huge egg-shaped head
he once fell off a wall himself

parts.answer: (c) — Think-Tank 'has a huge, egg-shaped head' and boasts of his 'balloon brain'.

parts.prompt: What does Think-Tank take the words 'Had a great fall!' to mean?
parts.answer: That the Earthlings plan to capture Mars Central Control and him — an invasion of Mars.

parts.prompt: Which quality of Think-Tank does this speech most clearly reveal?

options.text: Cowardice — his first thought is his own escape
Courage in the face of danger
Concern for the safety of the Earthlings
Patience in studying the evidence

parts.answer: (a) — 'Noodle, prepare a space capsule for me. I must escape without delay.'

parts.prompt: How does this misreading end up saving the Earth? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: Believing Mars is about to be invaded, Think-Tank orders the crew to leave Earth and the invasion fleet to evacuate Mars for Alpha Centauri. So the Martian invasion of Earth never happens. (1 mark: his orders to flee; 1 mark: the invasion called off.)

questions.extract:
THINK-TANK: Well? Well? Report to me. What do you hear?
OMEGA: Nothing, sir. Perhaps we are not on the correct frequency.
IOTA: Nothing, sir. Perhaps the Earthlings have sharper ears than we do.
OOP: I don't hear a thing. Maybe these sandwiches don't make sounds.
THINK-TANK: What? Does somebody suggest the Mighty Think-Tank has made a mistake?
OMEGA: Oh, no, sir; no, sir. We'll keep listening.
NOODLE: Please excuse me, your Brilliance, but a cloudy piece of information is twirling around in my head.
THINK-TANK: Well, twirl it out, Noodle, and I will clarify it for you.
NOODLE: I seem to recall that the Earthlings did not listen to the sandwiches; they opened them and watched them.

parts.prompt: Omega and Iota explain why they hear nothing by suggesting the wrong frequency or sharper Earthling ears. Their explanations show that they

options.text: avoid suggesting that Think-Tank's order was mistaken
have understood what books really are
want to return to Mars at once
are making fun of Sergeant Oop

parts.answer: (a) — they find excuses rather than say the order was wrong.

parts.prompt: Which crew member comes closest to stating plainly that the 'sandwiches' make no sound?
parts.answer: Sergeant Oop ('Maybe these sandwiches don't make sounds.').

parts.prompt: 'Well, twirl it out, Noodle, and I will clarify it for you.' This line is amusing because

options.text: Noodle is not allowed to speak at all
Think-Tank already knows what Noodle will say
Think-Tank will present Noodle's correct idea as his own clarification
Noodle's information turns out to be wrong

parts.answer: (c) — he then says 'Yes, that is quite correct, I will clarify that for you' and announces 'eye communication' as his own idea.

parts.prompt: What does Omega's hurried reply, 'Oh, no, sir; no, sir. We'll keep listening.', reveal about life at Mars Space Control? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: The crew are afraid to contradict Think-Tank, even when his order plainly is not working; they would rather carry on with something pointless.
